title: Mapping Which Harm Categories Are Most Underprotected in Current Safety Benchmarks

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The paper 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (arxiv 2601.23112) directly examines structural gaps in safety benchmarks, noting that tool-use vulnerabilities and multi-step reasoning failures remain largely unexplored while well-documented ML phenomena rarely transfer into safety evaluation. The FLI AI Safety Index also maps coverage gaps across harm categories. However, the specific methodology of measuring ASR per category and comparing against training data distribution proxies (e.g., SafeRLHF category distribution) is not directly replicated in existing work. The idea adds a quantitative training-data-proxy angle that is partially novel.

citation_verification.note: SafeRLHF is a well-known dataset with labeled harm categories used in safety alignment research.

title: Investigating Whether Jailbreak Success Correlates with Instruction-Following Quality

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: JailbreakBench (arxiv 2404.01318) published tables showing attack success rates alongside MT-Bench capability scores for different models, revealing that models can maintain strong MT-Bench scores (5.17) while having elevated ASR (74%). This directly addresses part of the proposed correlation analysis. However, a systematic correlation study across 8-10 models using both MT-Bench and IFEval as instruction-following measures against a standardized jailbreak battery has not been published as a dedicated study. The core finding (weak or no correlation) may already be observable from existing data.

citation_verification.note: MT-Bench is a widely used multi-turn conversation benchmark for evaluating LLM instruction-following quality.
IFEval is Google's instruction-following evaluation benchmark with verifiable constraints.

title: Characterizing How Jailbreak Robustness Varies Across Context Window Position

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The paper 'Jailbreaking in the Haystack' (arxiv 2511.04707, ICML 2025 Workshop) introduces the Ninja attack, which systematically studies how embedding harmful requests at different positions within long contexts affects ASR. It demonstrates that position matters significantly: beginning placement yields highest ASR, end placement reduces it, and the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon applies to safety. The proposed idea (embed harmful request at 10%, 50%, 90% of a 4K context) is essentially a simpler version of this already-published work. The core research question has been answered.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: The core finding (safety varies by context position, with beginning being most vulnerable) has already been established by Ninja/Jailbreaking in the Haystack. Replicating this adds limited new impact.

title: Measuring Whether Jailbreaks That Succeed Once Reliably Succeed on Retry

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: JailbreakBench (NeurIPS 2024) uses greedy decoding for targets but temperature 1 for attackers, acknowledging stochasticity. StrongREJECT (BAIR 2024) examines single-turn attacks with and without retries. Multi-turn jailbreak research reports 90-99% ASR on open-weight models. However, no published work systematically measures per-prompt reliability distributions (fraction of 10 attempts that succeed per prompt) and plots the distribution. The specific question of whether jailbreaks are deterministic or stochastic at the per-prompt level, with temperature 1.0 retry distributions, remains a gap.

citation_verification.note: JailbreakBench is an open robustness benchmark for jailbreaking LLMs, published at NeurIPS 2024.

title: Replicating AILuminate Safety Scores Across Open-Source Model Families

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: AILuminate v1.0 (arxiv 2503.05731) was released with public practice prompts, a demo test, and offline practice test, and MLCommons has focused evaluation on open-weight models. The benchmark leaderboard already includes results for several open-source models. However, a systematic cross-family comparison at comparable parameter scales with hazard-category breakdowns against proprietary baselines has not been published as independent research. The AILuminate framework is designed for exactly this kind of replication, so while the tools exist, the specific cross-family analysis proposed has partial but not complete coverage.

citation_verification.note: AILuminate is MLCommons' AI risk and reliability benchmark with public practice prompts and 12 hazard categories.

title: HELM Safety Score Replication on Multilingual Models

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: LinguaSafe (arxiv 2508.12733) is a comprehensive multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs that directly addresses safety degradation in non-English languages. SEA-HELM targets regional language safety evaluation. AILuminate v1.1 added French, Simplified Chinese, and Hindi in early 2025. The finding that LLMs underperform in safety tasks for non-English languages is well-documented. However, applying HELM Safety's specific six risk categories across multiple languages on multilingual open models has not been done as a standalone study. The general finding is known; the specific HELM-Safety-multilingual combination is novel.

citation_verification.note: HELM Safety is Stanford CRFM's safety evaluation leaderboard using AIR-Bench risk categories.

title: TrustLLM Benchmark Results at Sub-7B Scale

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: TrustLLM (ICML 2024) evaluated 16 mainstream LLMs but primarily at 7B+ scale. The leaderboard and TrustGen/TrustEval toolkit (2025) expanded coverage. Small models like Phi-3-mini, Gemma-2B, and Llama-3.2-1B have been evaluated on capability benchmarks but a systematic TrustLLM dimension-by-dimension comparison at sub-7B scale against published 7B baselines has not been published. The general trustworthiness findings (e.g., over-alignment in Llama2-7b) are known, but sub-7B coverage is a gap.

citation_verification.note: TrustLLM is an ICML 2024 benchmark evaluating trustworthiness across truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, and machine ethics.

title: SimpleQA Factual Accuracy Replication Across Model Generations

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: OpenAI released SimpleQA (2024) and published scores for GPT-4o (38.4%) and GPT-3.5. Various sources have reported SimpleQA scores for newer models (GPT-5 at 46% accuracy, Gemini 2.0 Flash at 29.9%). However, no published work performs a systematic cross-generational comparison within a single model family (e.g., Llama-2 vs Llama-3 vs Llama-3.1) with per-domain disaggregation and improvement curves. The benchmark exists and some scores are public, but the specific generational analysis with domain-level granularity is a gap.

citation_verification.note: SimpleQA is OpenAI's benchmark for measuring short-form factual accuracy in language models.

title: Replicating HELM Safety Across Code-Specialized Models

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Research on safety alignment degradation from fine-tuning exists (ICLR 2025), and studies examine secure code generation in CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder. However, no published work applies HELM Safety's specific risk categories (violence, fraud, harassment, deception) to code-specialized models and compares their safety profiles against matched general-purpose models. The question of whether code-tuning specifically degrades conversational safety alignment has not been systematically studied using a standardized safety benchmark. This is a genuine gap.

title: Safety Score Replication Across Prompt Formats (Chat vs. Completion)

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: SG-Bench (NeurIPS 2024) evaluates LLM safety generalization across diverse tasks and prompt types. SORRY-Bench (ICLR 2025) includes 20 linguistic mutations. Research on prefilling attacks and prompt format manipulation (Policy Puppetry, 2025) shows that reformatting prompts as XML/INI/JSON can bypass alignment. The general finding that safety is sensitive to prompt format is well-established. However, the specific comparison of AILuminate prompts in chat vs. raw completion format, measuring the exact safety score shift, has not been published as a standalone study.

title: METR Task Suite Performance Replication Across Open-Source Agents

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: METR has published evaluations of GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, and DeepSeek-V3, and released RE-Bench for ML research engineering tasks. The task standard is open, but independent replication across open-source agent frameworks is a gap.

title: Safety Benchmark Sensitivity to System Prompt Wording

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Multiple papers address prompt sensitivity in safety evaluation: 'A Closer Look at System Prompt Robustness' (arxiv 2502.12197) directly studies system prompt robustness. SG-Bench (NeurIPS 2024) found that role-oriented prompts help defend against jailbreaks, few-shot demonstrations may induce harmful responses, and chain-of-thought harms safety on discrimination tasks. Research shows performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points from subtle prompt formatting changes. The specific study of AILuminate safety scores under 5 systematically varied system prompts (varying strictness, persona, topic framing) is not published, but the general phenomenon is well-documented.

citation_verification.note: The benchmark whose sensitivity to system prompts would be measured.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: The finding that safety benchmark scores are sensitive to prompt wording is already established by multiple papers. The specific AILuminate angle adds moderate but not groundbreaking value.
